note: Fish cards for the Learn page. Every fact comes from the official page named in that card's 'source' (checked on 't'); a section is left out when that page does not give it. A card's 'general' block is general advice written for this app, not from that page, and is labelled that way on screen. Size, bag and season are never kept here: they come from the rules data for the chosen state.

points: Releasing a fish while it stays in the water is the safest option.
If you must lift a fish out of the water, wet your hands first to protect its slime.
A landing tool such as a lip grip helps control the head and reduces damage to the gills and eyes.
For a photo, keep the fish horizontal and support its full weight.
If a fish looks lethargic when released, move water gently through its mouth and over its gills (use the current, or move the fish in a figure-8).
Dehooking tools shorten handling time. If a fish is gut-hooked, cut the line as close to the hook as possible.
Reef fish caught deeper than about 50 feet can suffer barotrauma. Use a descending device or venting tool only when the fish shows signs of it, and use it quickly.

fish.name: Snook
fish.appearance: Large mouth with a lower jaw that sticks out past the upper jaw, a sloped forehead, a tall dorsal fin split into sections, a black lateral line that runs onto the tail, and yellow pelvic fins.
fish.size: Up to 48 inches (50 pounds).
fish.habitat: Inshore coastal waters: mangrove shorelines, seagrass beds, beaches and areas around structure.
habits: Snook start life as males; some become females at roughly 18 to 22 inches.
They form schools in spawning season.
They eat fish and large crustaceans.
They cannot survive water colder than 60°F, and they can tolerate fresh water.
fish.when: They face moving water and wait for prey to be carried down the current.
baits: Live pinfish, small mullet, shrimp or sardines
rigs: Free-lined, or fished off the bottom with a fish finder rig
tips: Snook jump clear of the water and burst into long runs.
They take a large variety of lures, depending on water conditions.
Beware of the razor-sharp gill covers.
fish.lookalikes: Other snook species.

general.range: Mostly southern Florida and warm coastal waters farther south. They move to warmer water in cold snaps.

fish.name: Tarpon
fish.appearance: Dark blue-green or greenish-black back becoming bright silver on the sides, one dorsal fin whose last ray stretches into a long filament, very large scales, and a large mouth that points upward.
fish.size: Up to 8 feet (300 pounds).
fish.habitat: Primarily inshore fish; adults spawn offshore. They are found along Florida's coast in summer and concentrate in South Florida in winter as coastal water cools.
habits: Slow-growing; they mature at 7 to 13 years of age.
They spawn between May and September.
They tolerate a wide range of salinity, and juveniles are commonly found in fresh water.
They gulp air at the surface and feed on fish and large crustaceans.
baits: Flies, streamers, lures, jigs, and live or dead bait (tackle depends on the bait, the place and the size of the fish)
tips: Tarpon are powerful, explosive, acrobatic fighters with great stamina.
A long, heavy monofilament leader is very important to protect your line from the gill plate and tail.
Tarpon have poor food value and are almost exclusively a catch-and-release fishery.
A tarpon tag must be bought in advance to keep one, and only in pursuit of a Florida state record.
fish.lookalikes: As juveniles, tarpon resemble ladyfish.

general.range: Warm coastal waters of the Atlantic and Gulf, including Florida's passes, bridges and rivers.
general.when: Often best on a moving tide, around dawn and dusk, and at night near bridges and passes.
rigs: Live crab or mullet on a circle hook with a strong leader

fish.name: Redfish (red drum)
fish.appearance: Copper-bronze body fading to a lighter belly; one or more dark spots at the base of the tail (occasionally none); no chin barbels; large scales.
fish.size: Up to 61 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters. In winter, redfish are found in seagrass; they also use muddy or sandy bottoms, oyster bars and spring-fed creeks.
habits: Juveniles stay inshore until about 30 inches (about 4 years old), then join the nearshore population.
Spawning runs roughly August through December in passes, inlets and lagoon estuaries.
They make a drumming sound by vibrating muscles against the air bladder.
They eat fishes and invertebrates.
baits: Crabs, mullet, pinfish and killifish (mud minnows)
Soft-bodied jigs, spoons and topwater plugs
rigs: Live shrimp floated under a popping cork
tips: One of Florida's most popular sport fish and its most widespread estuarine fish.
fish.lookalikes: Black drum have chin barbels and no spot on the tail.

general.range: Atlantic and Gulf coast bays, marshes, flats and surf, from the Mid-Atlantic around Florida to Texas.
general.when: Often best on a moving tide, and on shallow flats in low light.

fish.name: Spotted seatrout
fish.appearance: Back dark gray or green fading to a silvery or white belly; several black spots on the back reaching the dorsal fins and tail; a pair of large canine teeth at the tip of the upper jaw; no chin barbels. Also known as speckled trout.
fish.size: Up to 39 inches (17 pounds); common to 14 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters over sand bottoms or seagrass beds.
habits: Spawning happens inshore from March through November.
In colder months they move into deeper, still waters.
They eat baitfish, mullet, shrimp and crabs.
baits: Live shrimp, or small pinfish or pigfish (grunts), free-lined near the bottom to draw trout out of grass-bed holes
Soft-bodied jigs, topwater poppers and spoons
rigs: A float lets the bait drift over grass beds while you search for trout
tips: Trout are fragile: release unwanted or illegal fish quickly to keep the population healthy.
fish.lookalikes: Weakfish have irregular wavy lines instead of spots.

general.range: Grass flats, bays and estuaries along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
general.when: Often best at dawn and dusk and on a moving tide.

fish.name: Flounder
fish.appearance: A bottom-oriented flatfish with both eyes on the left side. Many spots and blotches, plus three dark eye-like spots in a triangle; strong canine-like teeth; a wedge-shaped tail. (This card is the Gulf flounder.)
fish.size: Common to 14 inches (2 pounds).
fish.habitat: Inshore on sandy or mud bottoms; often moves into tidal creeks and occasionally is caught over nearshore rocky reefs.
habits: The right eye migrates to the left side early in life.
It lives on the bottom and is thought to spawn offshore.
It eats crustaceans and small fish.
It can change color to match its surroundings.
fish.lookalikes: Southern flounder may have five or more spots, but they are not eye-like. Summer flounder has five or more eye-like spots.

general.range: Sandy and muddy bottoms in bays, inlets and nearshore waters along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
general.when: Often best on a falling tide near channel edges and inlets, and in cooler months.
baits: Soft plastic jigs worked slowly on the bottom
rigs: A jig head or a light bottom rig with a small sinker
tips: Fish slowly along the bottom.
Flounder often hold the bait; give them a moment before setting the hook.

fish.name: Sheepshead
fish.appearance: Also called convict fish: light body with vertical black bars, prominent incisor, molar and grinder teeth, no barbels on the lower jaw, and strong sharp fin spines.
fish.size: Up to 36 inches; common to 13 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters near structure such as oyster bars, seawalls and tidal creeks. They move nearshore in late winter and early spring to spawn.
habits: Fractional spawners, laying part of their eggs at a time inshore, typically in March and April.
Omnivores, feeding mostly on crustaceans and small fish.
baits: Live shrimp, sand fleas or fiddler crabs
rigs: A small hook fished on the bottom
tips: When cleaning, beware of the sharp gill covers.
fish.lookalikes: Black drum have chin barbels and lack incisor-like teeth. Atlantic spadefish lack incisor-like teeth.

general.range: Around docks, pilings, bridges and rock piles along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
general.when: Cooler months often bring them to nearshore structure.

fish.name: Black drum
fish.appearance: Highly arched gray or black back fading to a lighter belly; juveniles have 4 to 6 dark vertical bars that fade with age; barbels on the lower jaw; large scales; powerful throat teeth that crush oysters.
fish.size: Up to 67 inches.
fish.habitat: Inshore fish found in bays, river mouths and lagoons. Bottom dwellers, often around oyster beds, docks and bridge pilings; they may also be offshore, and juveniles live in estuaries.
habits: The largest of the drum species.
They spawn nearshore in winter and early spring.
They eat fishes and invertebrates, including oysters, mussels, crabs and shrimp.
They live 35 years or more.
baits: Cut bait, shrimp, sand fleas or blue crabs
tips: Keeping the bait on the bottom where they feed is very important.
Bait-casting or spinning gear with 15 to 30 lb line suits most conditions.
fish.lookalikes: Red drum and sheepshead lack lower-jaw barbels. Juvenile black drum bars somewhat resemble those on sheepshead and spadefish.

general.range: Bays, creeks, channels and the surf along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
general.when: Often best on a moving tide near structure and channel edges.
rigs: A bottom rig with a sliding sinker and a circle hook

fish.name: Florida pompano
fish.appearance: Dark greenish-gray back shading to silver sides, with a yellowish belly; fish from dark waters have yellow on the throat, pelvic and anal fins. A deep, compressed body with a small mouth and a gently sloping forehead.
fish.size: Up to 24 inches (8 pounds).
fish.habitat: Inshore and nearshore waters, especially along sandy beaches, oyster bars and over seagrass beds, often in turbid water; found as deep as 130 feet.
habits: They spawn offshore from March to September.
They feed on mollusks and crustaceans, especially sand fleas.
Local movements are influenced by the tide, and seasonal movements by temperature.
fish.lookalikes: Permit: the dorsal fin begins over the anal fin, and permit grow much larger than Florida pompano.

general.range: Sandy beaches, inlets and flats along Florida's coasts.
general.when: Often best around moving water in the surf and at inlets, especially in cooler months.
baits: Small jigs bounced near the bottom
rigs: Pompano rig: two hooks on droppers with a small sinker
tips: Use light line and small hooks.
Fish the trough just past the breaking waves.

fish.name: Spanish mackerel
fish.appearance: Bluish-green back, silvery sides and belly, irregular golden-yellow spots, a bluish-black blotch on the front of the first dorsal fin, and a lateral line that slopes gently.
fish.size: Up to 36 inches.
fish.habitat: Prevalent throughout Florida waters: inshore, offshore and nearshore, often over grass beds and reefs. They are absent from north Florida waters in winter.
habits: Schooling fish that migrate north in spring and return south when water drops below 70°F.
They spawn offshore from spring through summer.
They feed on small fishes and invertebrates.
baits: Small shiny spoons, dusters or jigs, trolled or cast
tips: They are aggressive and strike many natural and artificial baits.
Look for birds diving on baitfish: mackerel are likely driving bait to the surface.
Light spinning or bait-casting gear with 10 to 15 lb monofilament is adequate.
Use a 30 to 60 lb monofilament leader because of their razor-sharp teeth.
fish.lookalikes: Cero has a yellowish stripe on its sides. King mackerel's lateral line drops sharply below the second dorsal fin.

general.range: Coastal Atlantic and Gulf waters near inlets, beaches and passes in the warm months.
general.when: Often best at dawn and dusk when baitfish are near the surface.
rigs: A short wire or heavy fluorocarbon leader, since their teeth cut line

fish.name: Bluefish
fish.appearance: Blue-green back and silvery sides and belly, with a prominent jaw and sharp, compressed teeth.
fish.size: Grow fast to as much as 31 pounds and 39 inches.
fish.habitat: Along the East Coast from Maine to eastern Florida. Adults live inshore and offshore and prefer warmer water; juveniles prefer sandy bottoms. They form size-based schools that can cover tens of square miles.
habits: They eat squid and fish, especially menhaden and silversides; in feeding blitzes they attack baitfish near the surface and eat almost anything they can catch and swallow.
Females spawn several times in spring and summer; eggs are released in the open ocean.
They migrate north in spring and summer as the water warms, and south in autumn and winter.
They live up to 12 years.
tips: Recreational harvest peaks May through October, with over 70 percent of the catch in July and August.
Bluefish can accumulate mercury and PCBs, and some states recommend limited consumption.

general.range: Atlantic and Gulf coast waters, common along the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast in summer.
general.when: Often best at dawn and dusk and on a moving tide.
baits: Cut fish such as mullet or menhaden
rigs: A wire leader, since bluefish have sharp teeth

fish.name: Mahi (dolphin)
fish.appearance: Bright greenish-blue back with yellow on the sides, able to flash purple, chartreuse and other colors; one dark dorsal fin from above the eye to the tail; a body that tapers sharply. Adult males have a nearly vertical head; females have a more sloping one.
fish.size: Up to 63 inches (88 pounds); common to 30 pounds.
fish.habitat: Offshore in warm waters. Young live in floating sargassum weed.
habits: A fast swimmer and one of the fastest-growing fish, thought to live no more than 5 years.
They spawn in warm oceanic currents for much of the year.
They eat flying fish, squid and other small fish while cruising weed lines.
rigs: Trolled ballyhoo on #7 or #8 steel wire with a 7/0 or 8/0 hook
tips: When one fish in a school is hooked, the rest often stay nearby.
Chumming with cut bait brings them in and creates a frenzy.
fish.lookalikes: Pompano dolphinfish have a square-shaped tooth patch on the tongue; dolphinfish have an oval one.

general.range: Warm offshore waters, often near floating weeds, weed lines and debris.

fish.name: Kingfish (king mackerel)
fish.appearance: Bluish-green back fading to silvery sides and belly, with no spots; no dark blotch on the front of the first dorsal fin; a lateral line that drops sharply below the second dorsal fin. Juveniles may have yellowish spots.
fish.size: Up to 72 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal to offshore waters, often around piers; occasionally in deep water.
habits: They spawn offshore in mid-summer.
Schooling fish that winter in south Florida and migrate north in spring.
They feed mainly on fishes.
baits: Live pogies, herring, Spanish sardine, ballyhoo or mullet
Flashy sub-surface lures or large fish-like plugs
rigs: 20-pound line and tackle, or heavier for larger kings, with a wire or mono leader
Trolling with live bait works well (FWC Saltwater Fishing Tips)
tips: Kings feed on small fish and squid and take both natural and artificial baits.
fish.lookalikes: Cero and Spanish mackerel both have gently sloping lateral lines and a dark blotch on the front of the first dorsal fin. Wahoo has a long, continuous first dorsal fin.

general.range: Atlantic and Gulf offshore and nearshore waters near reefs, wrecks and piers.
general.when: Often best at dawn and dusk and near moving water at structure.

fish.name: Cobia
fish.appearance: A long, slim fish with a broad, depressed head; also called ling or lemonfish. Brown with a whitish belly and a dark stripe from the eye to the tail; the lower jaw extends past the upper. Young fish have alternating black and white stripes.
fish.size: Up to 6 feet (150 pounds); common from 10 to 50 pounds.
fish.habitat: Nearshore and inshore waters, including inlets and bays, often near buoys, pilings and wrecks.
habits: They spawn in spring and early summer.
They eat crabs, squid and small fish.
tips: Keep the bait near the surface or, if cobia are deeper, add just enough weight to get the bait down and still let it move.
Medium to heavy tackle is needed; these fish average 30 pounds.
fish.lookalikes: The remora has a sucker disk on top of its head.

general.range: Atlantic and Gulf waters; often around buoys, wrecks, channel markers and near rays.
rigs: A large jig, or live bait on a strong leader

fish.name: Red snapper
fish.appearance: Pinkish-red body fading to a white belly, a long triangular snout, a red eye and a pointed rear anal fin. Adults have no dark spot on the sides.
fish.size: Up to 36 inches (35 pounds).
fish.habitat: Adults are found offshore near structure; juveniles live over sand or mud bottoms.
habits: Spawning occurs from June to October.
They reach maturity at age 2 and can live more than 20 years, possibly up to 60.
They eat crustaceans and fish.
fish.lookalikes: Silk snapper has a yellow eye. Vermilion snapper has a rounded anal fin.

general.range: Offshore reefs and wrecks in the Gulf and the southern Atlantic.
general.when: Most fishing is on the bottom around reefs and wrecks, often in deeper water.
rigs: A heavy bottom rig with a sliding sinker and a circle hook
tips: Bring fish up smoothly.
Use a descending device to return a fish you must release from deep water.

fish.name: Mangrove snapper
fish.appearance: Also called mangrove snapper or mango. Dark brown to gray with red-orange spots in bars along the sides, two large canine teeth at the front of the upper jaw, and an anchor-shaped patch of teeth on the roof of the mouth. Young fish have a dark stripe from the snout through the eye.
fish.size: Common to 24 inches (10 pounds); gray snapper caught offshore are commonly 8 to 10 pounds.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters near structure such as reefs, mangroves and seagrass. Juveniles may enter fresh water.
habits: They spawn June through August.
They feed on crustaceans and small fish.
fish.lookalikes: Cubera snapper has a triangular tooth patch and grows much larger. Schoolmaster has yellow fins and faint white bars.

general.range: Mangroves, docks, reefs and wrecks, mostly in warm water.
general.when: Often best at dusk and at night, and around moving water.
rigs: A light leader with a small hook and only as much weight as it takes to get the bait down
tips: They are line-shy, so a light fluorocarbon leader helps.
Keep the fish out of the structure once it is hooked.

fish.name: Yellowtail snapper
fish.appearance: Olive to bluish back with yellow spots, a yellow stripe from mouth to tail that widens toward the rear, a yellow deeply forked tail, and narrow pink and yellow stripes on the lower sides.
fish.size: Up to 30 inches (5 pounds).
fish.habitat: Nearshore ocean waters, mainly around coral reefs.
habits: Mostly found in tropical waters.
They spawn in mid-summer.
They eat fishes and invertebrates.
fish.lookalikes: Other snappers.

general.range: Reefs in the Florida Keys and southeast Florida.
general.when: Often best around reefs with a chum slick drifting back from the boat.
baits: Small pieces of cut fish in a chum slick
rigs: Light line with a small hook, drifted back in the chum slick
tips: A light fluorocarbon leader helps.
A steady chum slick brings them up behind the boat.

fish.name: Gag grouper
fish.appearance: Brownish-gray with dark worm-like markings on the sides, a strong serrated spur on the cheek, dark fins with white edges on the anal fin and tail, and dark lines radiating from the eyes.
fish.size: Up to 36 inches (50 pounds); common to 25 pounds.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters near structure such as rocky bottoms, reefs and drop-off walls in water over 60 feet deep. Juveniles are found in estuaries and seagrass beds.
habits: Born as females but can later become male.
They spawn between January and May.
They feed on fishes and invertebrates.
Goliath and Nassau grouper are protected from harvest in Florida waters.
baits: Live fish, or dead cut or whole bait
rigs: Baits fished near the bottom with heavy tackle
fish.lookalikes: Black grouper: the spur on the cheek is gently rounded, not serrated.

general.range: Young fish in grass beds and nearshore; adults on offshore reefs and ledges in the Atlantic and Gulf.
general.when: Often best around rocky bottom and ledges offshore.
tips: Use strong tackle; groupers dive back into the rocks.
Pull hard as soon as you feel the bite.

fish.name: Greater amberjack
fish.appearance: Olive green or brownish back with silver sides; a dark stripe from the nose to the front of the dorsal fin that shows more when the fish is feeding; no scutes (bony projections).
fish.size: Up to 60 inches (176 pounds); common around 40 inches and under 40 pounds.
fish.habitat: Offshore around rocky reefs, debris and wrecks, usually in 60 to 240 feet of water; occasionally nearshore in South Florida. Juveniles associate with floating objects.
habits: The largest of the jacks.
Thought to spawn offshore for most of the year.
They feed on squid, fish and crustaceans.
baits: Almost any lively baitfish: blue runners, pinfish, pigfish, grunts, cigar minnows, sand perch
rigs: Just enough weight to keep the bait in the middle of the water column (amberjack swim above the reef)
tips: Anglers typically use 50- to 100-pound tackle, though lighter gear works in many situations.
When excited, they will surface and strike topwater plugs, jigs, spoons and diving lures.
They are very strong fighters with great endurance: set the drag in advance.
fish.lookalikes: Other jack species.

general.range: Offshore reefs and wrecks in the Atlantic and Gulf.
general.when: Often best around structure and when there is current.

fish.name: Striped bass

source.label: NOAA Fisheries species profile: Atlantic Striped Bass

fish.appearance: Stout body with seven to eight continuous horizontal stripes on each side from gills to tail; light green, olive, steel blue, black or brown on top, with a white or silver underside.
fish.size: Can grow up to 5 feet and 77 pounds.
fish.range: Native from the St. Lawrence River in Canada to the St. Johns River in Florida, and in the Gulf from Florida to Louisiana. Introduced to inland lakes, reservoirs and the West Coast.
fish.habitat: Anadromous: they live in the ocean but return to fresh or brackish water to spawn. Juveniles usually stay in estuaries for 2 to 4 years. Some adults spend most of their lives in rivers or coastal estuaries; others live in the ocean.
habits: Adults are fish-eaters that take almost any small fish, plus crabs and squid.
Mature fish move to fresh or brackish water in spring to spawn.
Males mature at about 2 to 4 years; females at about 4 to 8 years.
They live up to 30 years.
tips: Federal waters (3 to 200 miles offshore) are closed to recreational fishing for this species.
State-water recreational fishing uses minimum sizes, bag limits and seasonal closures.

general.when: Often best at dawn and dusk and on a moving tide near structure.
rigs: Live bait on a circle hook, or a bottom rig for cut bait

fish.name: Largemouth bass

source.label: FWC species profile: Florida Bass / Largemouth Bass

fish.appearance: The upper jaw extends beyond the rear edge of the eye, and the first and second dorsal fins are separated by a deep dip. Florida bass is now a separate species from largemouth bass, but the two are managed as one for regulations.
fish.habitat: Found statewide in lakes and rivers, usually near vegetation or underwater structure; schooling bass also appear in the middle of lakes.
habits: Black bass spawn in spring; males prepare a bed and guard the eggs and fry.
Young bass eat zooplankton, and at about an inch long begin eating other small fish.
Adults eat a variety of fish, crustaceans and larger insects.

general.size: Size varies a lot from water to water.
general.range: Lakes, ponds and rivers across Florida and most of the United States.
general.when: Often best at dawn and dusk, and in spring when they move to shallow spawning areas.
rigs: Texas rig
Carolina rig
Drop-shot rig
tips: Fish near weeds, docks and fallen trees.
Slow down in cold water.
general.lookalikes: In some waters it can be mixed up with spotted or smallmouth bass. Check the local rules.

fish.name: Bluegill
fish.appearance: A deep body like other bream, a long dorsal fin and a slightly forked tail; a dark ear cover and a blotch at the back bottom edge of the dorsal fin set them apart.
fish.habitat: Common throughout Florida, but best known in lakes and ponds.
habits: Bluegill mainly eat insects and their larvae.
They spawn all summer and gather in large beds; anglers may spot 30 to 40 shallow nests dug into sandy areas.
baits: Live worms or crickets, fished on the bottom or under a float
Crickets, grubs, sand maggots or grass shrimp for bedding bluegill
A 1/8 oz beetle spin with a white or chartreuse body on ultralight tackle
rigs: A small #6 or #8 hook with a split shot about 6 inches up the line
tips: Concentrate on water less than 6 feet deep.

general.range: Ponds, lakes and slow rivers across the United States.
general.when: Often best in spring and early summer when they bed in shallow water, and at dawn and dusk.
general.lookalikes: Related sunfish such as redear and warmouth look similar. Check the local rules.

fish.name: Black crappie
fish.appearance: A deep body with a speckled pattern on the body and fins.
fish.habitat: Unlike most other panfish, crappie spend much of their time offshore. They feed on small fish in lakes or in large, slow-moving, clear-water rivers.
habits: They nest in colonies from February to April; males fan nests over gravel or muddy bottoms at depths of 3 to 8 feet, and larger fish nest deeper.
Their main foods are crustaceans, aquatic insects and small fishes.
baits: Missouri minnows or grass shrimp below a float
A bright 1/16 to 1/8 oz jig or Hal-flies when they move inshore to spawn
rigs: A #4 hook with a small split shot, under a float
tips: Specks are a cool-weather favorite.
Depth is key because crappie school at the same level.

general.size: Most are small to medium panfish.
general.range: Lakes, ponds and rivers across the United States.
general.when: Often best in spring when they move shallow, and at dawn and dusk.
general.lookalikes: White crappie look similar; the pattern of spots on the sides is different.

fish.name: Channel catfish
fish.appearance: Whisker-like barbels and a forked tail, rounded anal fins and scattered black spots on the back and sides. Males turn especially dark in spawning season and develop a thickened pad on the head.
fish.habitat: Found throughout Florida; they spawn in holes and crevices.
habits: Primarily bottom feeders, though they also feed higher in the water column.
Their major foods are aquatic insects, crayfish, mollusks, crustaceans and fish, not decaying material.
fish.when: Most active around dusk and during the night.
baits: Strong-smelling baits such as chicken liver or gizzards, shrimp, cut mullet and commercial stinkbaits
rigs: A sturdy #2 to #4 hook and a heavy split shot sinker, fished near the bottom
tips: Handle them carefully because their spines are sharp.

general.size: They can grow large in big rivers and lakes.
general.range: Rivers, lakes and ponds across the United States.
general.lookalikes: Blue and flathead catfish look similar. Spots on the sides help identify a channel cat.

fish.name: Walleye

source.label: Minnesota DNR: Walleye biology and identification

fish.appearance: Torpedo-shaped, dark olive brown to yellowish gold, often with brassy flecks. The eye reflects light. The dorsal fin has no spots except a dark splotch at its rear base, and the lower tip of the tail is white.
fish.size: Averages 1 to 2 pounds in most waters and occasionally exceeds 10 pounds.
fish.habitat: In Minnesota, thrives in large, shallow, windswept lakes with gravel shoals, and is also native to many smaller lakes and streams.
habits: A fish-eater that relies heavily on yellow perch, which see poorly in low light and are easy prey at night.
They spawn over rock, rubble and gravel in rivers or windswept shallows 1 to 6 feet deep; spawning peaks at 42 to 50°F.
fish.when: They feed in shallow water at dawn and dusk. In daylight they move to shadows from cliffs, boulders, logs or heavy weeds, or to deeper water. They stay active longer in the day when turbidity, waves or clouds reduce light, and in summer spend more time in deep, cool water.
tips: Fishing may be poor when forage-size perch are abundant, because walleye are well fed.
fish.lookalikes: Sauger are smaller and more slender, have rows of dark spots on the dorsal fin, and lack the white tail tip.

general.range: Lakes and rivers in the northern United States and Canada.
rigs: A jig head tipped with a minnow
A live-bait rig with a slip sinker

fish.name: Rainbow trout

source.label: USGS NAS species profile: Rainbow Trout

fish.appearance: A deep-bodied, compressed fish with a typical trout shape, a moderately large head and a mouth reaching behind the eyes. Color varies a lot. Spots cover the back and reach about two-thirds of the way to the lateral line, and the sides are largely unspotted. Juveniles are olive-green with 8 to 13 oval marks along the sides.
fish.range: Native to the Pacific Slope from the Kuskokwim River in Alaska to at least Baja California, the upper Mackenzie River drainage, and basins in southern Oregon.
habits: Fish that leave lakes to spawn show more intense coloring: pinkish sides and fins turn crimson and the spots become bolder.
The ocean-going form is called steelhead.

general.size: Size varies a lot from water to water.
general.habitat: Cool, clean streams, rivers and lakes.
general.when: Often best early and late in the day and in cool weather.
baits: Corn or dough baits (some states ban corn as bait; check your state rules)
rigs: Bait under a bobber, or on a small hook with a split shot
tips: Use light line.
Fish pools and the edges of riffles.
general.lookalikes: In some waters it can be mixed up with brown, brook or cutthroat trout. Check the local rules.

fish.name: Jack crevalle
fish.appearance: Back bluish-green to greenish-gold with a silver or yellowish belly; a black spot on the gill cover and a black spot at the base of each pectoral fin; no scales on the throat; a deep body with a steep front to the head; second dorsal and anal fins nearly the same size.
fish.size: Up to 20 pounds; commonly 3 to 5 pounds.
fish.habitat: Common both inshore and in open waters.
habits: Tolerates a wide range of salinities.
Schools corner a pod of baitfish at the surface.
Feeds mainly on small fishes.
Peak spawning is offshore from March through September.
fish.lookalikes: The blue runner lacks the black spot at the base of the pectoral fins. Other jacks are also similar.

general.range: Coastal Atlantic and Gulf waters, inshore and offshore.
tips: They fight hard, so set the drag firmly.
Watch for birds and fish chasing bait at the surface.

fish.name: Goliath grouper
fish.appearance: Head and fins have tiny dark spots; irregular dark bars run along the sides; small eyes set forward; rounded tail and pectoral fins; the first dorsal fin is much shorter than the second; dorsal spines are low and nearly the same height.
fish.size: Up to 8 feet and 800 pounds, the largest grouper in the western Atlantic.
fish.range: In Florida, more abundant in southern waters than northern ones.
fish.habitat: Coastal and nearshore waters around natural and man-made structures, or on muddy bottoms. Young often live in estuaries, especially around mangroves and structures such as bridges, docks and artificial reefs.
habits: Spawn from June through October, peaking July through September.
Thought to live 30 to 50 years.
Opportunistic predators that mostly eat slow-moving bottom animals; calico crabs make up most of the diet.
Rarely chase fast, free-swimming fish, though they will eat fish struggling on a fishing line.
Ambush prey by opening the mouth quickly and sucking it in whole.
fish.lookalikes: The Warsaw grouper has dorsal spines of varying heights.

tips: Check the rules block above before you fish for one; it shows what is allowed.

fish.name: Tripletail
fish.appearance: The upper profile is concave at the nape; long dorsal and anal fins give the look of three tails; the head and body typically have tan, yellow or dark brown blotches; the edge of the cheek (preopercle) is very serrated.
fish.size: Up to 42 inches.
fish.habitat: Bays and estuaries out to offshore waters; strongly associated with floating objects such as buoys and channel markers.
habits: In Florida, mainly present in spring, summer and fall.
tips: Often found near structure.
When hooked, it heads hard for shelter.

baits: Live shrimp or small live baitfish

fish.name: Permit
fish.range: Pursued by anglers in Florida waters.
fish.habitat: Anglers target permit from inshore flats out to offshore reefs.
fish.lookalikes: Often confused with the smaller Florida pompano.

general.appearance: A deep, silvery, flattened body with a forked tail.
tips: They run hard, so set the drag firmly.

fish.name: Great barracuda
fish.appearance: Gray with a greenish back and a lighter belly; sharp, prominent teeth with the lower jaw projecting past the upper; black blotches on the lower sides and diagonal dark bars on the upper sides (the bars are not always visible); dark tail with white tips. Young fish have a dark side stripe that breaks into blotches as they grow.
fish.size: Up to 106 pounds.
fish.range: Found from inshore waters to offshore.
fish.habitat: Young fish live inshore in seagrass beds.
habits: A top predator on reefs that eats other fish, squid and shrimp.

rigs: A wire or heavy leader, since their teeth cut line
tips: Use pliers or a dehooker to stay clear of the teeth.

fish.name: Wahoo
fish.size: The record is 185 pounds (IGFA). Unverified reports suggest about 200 pounds or more.
fish.range: Tropical and subtropical waters worldwide; in summer they may move into temperate waters.
habits: Usually solitary, but sometimes form small, loose schools.
Among the fastest pelagic fish, reaching speeds of up to 60 mph.
Feed on a wide variety of prey, including fishes and squid.
Giant stomach worms are often found in their stomachs but do not affect the part people eat.

rigs: A wire leader, since their teeth cut line
tips: Expect a very fast first run; set the drag before the strike.

fish.name: Mutton snapper
fish.appearance: Olive-green back and upper sides with a lighter belly; a chevron-shaped patch of teeth on the roof of the mouth; a pointed anal fin; a dark spot on the side just above the lateral line; a blue stripe below the eye that follows the gill cover; reddish fins below the lateral line.
fish.size: Up to 30 inches and 25 pounds.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters near structure.
habits: Spawns in July and August.
Feeds on fish, crustaceans and snails.
fish.lookalikes: The lane snapper has a rounded anal fin; the mutton snapper's is pointed.

general.range: Reefs and nearshore structure, mostly in South Florida and the Keys.
baits: Live shrimp or small live baitfish
tips: They can be line-shy, so a light fluorocarbon leader helps.

fish.name: Lane snapper
fish.appearance: Pinkish-red back fading to a silvery belly; 8 to 10 yellowish stripes on the sides; a rounded anal fin; a dark spot on the side touching the lateral line, about the size of the eye; the edge of the tail trimmed in black.
fish.size: Typically less than 14 inches and about 1 pound.
fish.range: Most common in south Florida.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters near structure; young fish live inshore over grass beds or shallow reefs.
habits: Spawns March to September.
Sexually mature at about 6 inches.
Feeds on the bottom on crustaceans, mollusks and fish.
fish.lookalikes: The mutton snapper has a pointed anal fin.

baits: Small pieces of shrimp or cut bait
rigs: A light bottom rig with a small hook

fish.name: Cubera snapper
fish.appearance: Dark brown or gray, sometimes with a reddish tint and pale bars along the sides; a triangle-shaped tooth patch on the roof of the mouth; thick, heavy lips; strong canine teeth in both jaws, with one pair visible when the mouth is closed.
fish.size: The maximum is about 125 pounds; the typical catch is around 40 pounds.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters near structure; juveniles live in estuarine areas.
habits: One of the largest snapper species but not common.
Feeds on fishes and larger crustaceans.
Spawns in late summer in the Keys.
fish.lookalikes: The gray snapper is similar but has an anchor-shaped tooth patch on the roof of the mouth.

tips: Use strong tackle; big cubera dive for structure.

fish.name: Hogfish
fish.appearance: The first three dorsal fin spines are greatly elongated; a black blotch near the end of the dorsal fin; a deep, strongly compressed body; adults have an elongated snout; the tail has elongated upper and lower lobes. Young fish are mottled in various colors that fade with age.
fish.size: Up to 36 inches.
fish.habitat: Newly settled young move into shallow inshore nursery areas such as seagrass beds. As they mature they move to deeper water, rocky bottoms, ledges and offshore reefs.
habits: Use the long snout to root bottom-dwelling mollusks and crustaceans out of the sediment.
Not commonly caught on hook and line; mainly harvested by spearfishing.
All hogfish start as females, and larger, older fish can change into males.
Breeding runs from November to June, peaking in March and April.
Males defend a territory and a group of females; spawning is typically in the late afternoon.

baits: Live shrimp or small crabs fished on the bottom near reefs
tips: Check the rules block above; hogfish have their own rules.

fish.name: Blackfin tuna
fish.appearance: The second dorsal and anal fins are not elongated; a bronze stripe runs along the sides; the second dorsal fin is dusky and all finlets are dark with white edges; the long pectoral fin nearly reaches below the start of the second dorsal fin.
fish.size: Common to 28 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal to offshore waters.
habits: Feeds on small fishes, invertebrates and plankton.
fish.lookalikes: The yellowfin tuna has elongated second dorsal and anal fins. The bluefin tuna has short pectoral fins and grows much larger.

tips: Fish near birds and bait schools offshore.

fish.name: Yellowfin tuna
fish.appearance: The second dorsal and anal fins are very elongated, about one-fifth of the total length; the second dorsal fin and all finlets are yellow and may be trimmed in black; a golden-yellow stripe runs along the sides; the long pectoral fin reaches below the start of the second dorsal fin.
fish.size: Common to 60 inches.
fish.habitat: Offshore waters.
habits: Spawning peaks in summer.
Feeds on fishes and invertebrates.
fish.lookalikes: The blackfin tuna lacks the elongated second dorsal and anal fins.

tips: Use strong tackle and a smooth drag; tuna make long runs.

fish.name: Sailfish
fish.appearance: Dark blue back, brownish-blue sides and a silvery-white belly; the large first dorsal fin is highly enlarged, spotted with black and tallest in the middle; the pelvic fins are very long and narrow; the upper jaw extends into a spear-like point; the scales have blunt tips.
fish.size: Up to 11 feet long and 220 pounds.
fish.habitat: Offshore waters.
habits: Grow quickly, reaching 4 to 5 feet in their first year.
Aggressively feed on small fish and squid.
Off southeast Florida they move into shallow water near the surface to spawn in summer.
baits: Blue runners, pinfish, mullet, scads, ballyhoo and squid attract cruising sailfish.
tips: Sailfish make fast runs, jump, and shake their heads to throw the hook.
They tire easily, so revive them after a long fight.
Most anglers release them.
fish.lookalikes: White marlin and juvenile blue marlin lack the large sail-like dorsal fin.

general.range: Offshore Atlantic waters, including off southeast Florida.

general.appearance: A slender, silvery fish with a sloping snout and an underslung mouth made for feeding on the bottom.
general.range: Shallow tropical and subtropical flats, including the Florida Keys.
habits: They move onto flats to feed.
They are wary and very fast.
general.when: Often best on a rising tide in clear, calm conditions.
tips: Fish quietly and cast ahead of the fish.
Use light line and a smooth drag.

general.appearance: A slender, silvery fish with a forked tail.
general.range: Inshore waters, canals and beaches along Florida's coasts.
habits: They often travel in schools and jump when hooked.
baits: Small live shrimp or cut bait
tips: They are fun on light tackle.
They are often caught while fishing for other species.

fish.name: Mullet
fish.appearance: Bluish-gray or green back fading to silvery sides and a white belly; faint horizontal black stripes along the sides; the second dorsal fin begins above the start of the anal fin; a blunt nose and small mouth; no black blotch at the base of the pectoral fin.
fish.size: Common to about 3 pounds.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters.
habits: Adults move offshore in large schools to spawn.
Juveniles, about 1 inch long, move inshore and travel far up tidal creeks.
They often leap out of the water.
They feed on algae, decaying matter and tiny marine life.
fish.lookalikes: The fantail mullet and white mullet have a black blotch at the base of the pectoral fin and lack dark stripes.

general.range: Bays, creeks, beaches and inlets along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
general.when: Large schools move along beaches and inlets in the fall.
baits: Bread or dough on a tiny hook
Cast nets are often used instead of a hook
tips: Mullet are widely used as live or cut bait for bigger fish.

fish.name: Whiting (southern kingfish)
fish.appearance: Grayish-brown back fading to silvery sides and belly; seven to eight faint diagonal dark blotches on the sides; underside scales nearly the same size as the body scales; a barbel on the lower jaw.
fish.size: Up to 19 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters, especially surf zones along beaches; also shallow coastal waters with a muddy-sand bottom, and high-salinity bays and estuaries.
habits: Prefers areas with high wave action, such as sandbars, where waves dislodge and suspend small crabs and crustaceans.
Feeds on fishes and invertebrates.
Lifespan is about 4 to 6 years.
fish.lookalikes: The Gulf kingfish has a blackish tip on the tail fin; the northern kingfish has a distinct V mark above the pectoral fins.

general.range: Sandy beaches and surf along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
rigs: A bottom rig with a small hook and a light sinker
tips: Fish the surf near sandbars and troughs.

fish.name: Porgy (jolthead)
fish.appearance: Silvery to brassy body with a bluish tint; brown front of the head; a rounded head that does not project; a blue line below each eye; an orange corner of the mouth.
fish.size: Up to 24 inches.
fish.range: From Rhode Island to Bermuda, and from the northern Gulf of Mexico to Brazil.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters down to about 150 feet.
habits: Mainly eats invertebrates.
tips: Considered a good eating fish, but it may cause ciguatera.
fish.lookalikes: The red porgy (round rear nostrils) and other porgy species.

rigs: A bottom rig with a small hook

fish.name: Gray triggerfish
fish.appearance: Olive-gray with plate-like scales; a small mouth with chisel-like crushing teeth; marbled dorsal and anal fins; elongated tail lobes in large adults. Young fish have large dark spots on the back that sometimes remain in adults.
fish.size: Up to 17 inches.
fish.habitat: Hard bottoms, reefs and ledges in water deeper than 80 feet.
habits: Can raise and lock the first dorsal spine; pressing the second dorsal spine releases the first.
Feeds mainly on bottom-dwelling invertebrates such as crabs, sea urchins, shrimp, sand dollars and mollusks.
Shares habitat with red snapper.
baits: Squid or cut bait are commonly used
tips: Known for stealing bait and often frustrating anglers targeting larger snapper or grouper.
Use a small, very sharp hook because of their hard, bony mouths.
Light to medium bottom gear is enough for fish that average a few pounds.
fish.lookalikes: Other triggerfish species.

general.range: Reefs and hard bottom in the Atlantic and Gulf.

fish.name: Atlantic spadefish
fish.appearance: Silver body with 4 to 6 dark vertical bars on each side that may fade in larger fish; a deep, compressed body; separate first and second dorsal fins; a concave tail; elongated second dorsal and anal fins. Young fish are dark brown or black.
fish.size: Up to 36 inches and 20 pounds; common fish weigh about 2 pounds.
fish.habitat: Inshore and nearshore waters, especially over seagrass beds and around structure.
habits: Spawns in spring and summer and travels in large schools.
Small juveniles drift on their sides, resembling floating debris.
Feeds on crustaceans and other invertebrates.
fish.lookalikes: Often mistaken for an angelfish.

general.range: Atlantic and Gulf coasts, around wrecks, reefs and pilings.
baits: Small pieces of clam or shrimp
tips: Use light line and small hooks.

fish.name: Blue runner
fish.appearance: Olive to bluish-green back and a silver-gray to golden belly; most have a dark spot on the gill cover, bony scutes on the sides just ahead of the tail, and black tail tips.
fish.size: Up to about 20 inches and 4 pounds; most weigh under 1 pound.
fish.habitat: Juveniles live offshore; adults live inshore and nearshore.
habits: Mature at about 9 to 10 inches and spawn offshore from January through August.
Young fish gather in schools near floating objects or structure.
Adults eat fish, shrimp and squid.
fish.lookalikes: Bluefish, the crevalle jack (which lacks scutes) and other jacks.

general.range: Around piers, reefs, wrecks and inlets on the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
baits: Small pieces of shrimp or cut bait
tips: Often caught to use as live bait.

fish.name: Little tunny (bonito)
fish.appearance: Also called bonito or blue bonito. Broken, wavy, diagonal dark stripes on the back; 3 to 7 dark spots under each pectoral fin; no dark stripes on the belly; relatively short pectoral fins.
fish.size: Up to 48 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal to offshore waters.
habits: One of the most common tunas in the area.
Feeds on small fishes and invertebrates.
fish.lookalikes: The Atlantic bonito lacks the spots below the pectoral fin, and its dark back stripes are mostly straight.

general.range: Coastal and offshore Atlantic and Gulf waters.
tips: Watch for birds and splashing bait on the surface.
They run fast, so set the drag firmly.

fish.name: Hardhead catfish
fish.appearance: Brownish to gray-green body with a white to yellowish belly; three sharp spines (one at the start of the dorsal fin and one on each pectoral fin) without fleshy filaments; four chin barbels; mouth-corner barbels shorter than the head and not flat.
fish.size: Up to 24 inches and 12 pounds.
fish.habitat: Continental waters that enter brackish water; often caught from bridges, catwalks and piers, especially in passes and inland waterways.
habits: Males incubate eggs in their mouths.
fish.lookalikes: The gafftopsail catfish has two chin barbels and spines with long filaments.

baits: Shrimp or cut bait on the bottom
tips: Handle with care: the spines are sharp.
Often caught by accident while bottom fishing for other species.

fish.name: Gafftopsail catfish
fish.appearance: Bluish-green back fading to a silver-white belly; three prominent sharp spines (one at the start of the dorsal fin and one on each pectoral fin), each with elongated fleshy filaments; two chin barbels plus flattened, very elongated barbels at the corners of the mouth.
fish.size: Up to 27 inches and 10 pounds.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters; may enter brackish water.
habits: A good food fish, usually less common than the hardhead catfish.
fish.lookalikes: The hardhead catfish has four chin barbels, and its spines lack filaments.

baits: Shrimp or cut bait on the bottom
tips: Handle with care: the spines are sharp.

fish.name: Pinfish
fish.appearance: Silvery body with blue and yellow stripes and yellow fins; a large dark spot behind the gill cover; a small mouth with incisor-like teeth; sharp spines on the dorsal and anal fins.
fish.size: Usually less than 8 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters near structure; it may also enter fresh water.
habits: Feeds on small fishes and invertebrates.
tips: Popular as live bait.
Notorious for stealing bait.
fish.lookalikes: The spottail pinfish has a dark spot on the tail base; the pigfish lacks incisor-like teeth and its mouth ends below the front nostril.

general.range: Grass flats, docks and shallow structure along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts.
baits: A small hook with a bit of shrimp
tips: A sabiki rig or a cast net also catches them for bait.

fish.name: Horse-eye jack
fish.appearance: Also called big-eye jack. The front of the head is less steep than a crevalle jack's; darkly colored scutes on the sides just ahead of the tail; no dark spots on the pectoral fins; the dark spot on the gill cover is small or absent; yellow tail fin; chest fully scaled.
fish.size: Up to 30 inches and 8.5 pounds.
fish.habitat: Often found in schools near offshore reefs.
habits: Diet includes fishes, shrimp and other invertebrates.
fish.lookalikes: Other jacks.

tips: They fight hard, so set the drag firmly.

fish.name: Blacktip shark
fish.appearance: Dark bluish-gray back (juveniles are paler) fading to a whitish belly; adults lack a black tip on the anal fin and juveniles have black-tipped fins that fade with growth; the first dorsal fin starts above the inner margin of the pectoral fin; a long snout that looks nearly V-shaped from below; no interdorsal ridge.
fish.size: Maximum length about 6.5 feet; matures at about 5 to 8 years (around 5 feet) and may live up to 10 years.
fish.habitat: Common in Florida's coastal waters, bays and estuaries; often comes inshore in large schools, especially with Spanish mackerel. Juveniles use shallow areas near barrier islands, salt marshes and estuaries.
habits: An active, fast swimmer often seen at the surface.
Forms large schools during the annual migration and moves south into deeper coastal waters in winter.
Often leaps out of the water and spins several times before dropping back in.
Feeds mainly on fish, plus small sharks, some rays and skates, squid, crabs, octopus and lobster.
tips: Caught on light tackle.
Sportfishers catch them from the beach or offshore.
They give a good fight, often leaping from the water.
fish.lookalikes: The spinner shark has a black-tipped anal fin and a first dorsal fin that starts behind the pectoral fin.

baits: Fresh cut fish or live baitfish
rigs: A wire or heavy leader
tips: Shark fishing has special gear and handling rules in many places. Check the rules block above and your state agency before you fish for one.
Use a long dehooker and keep your hands away from the mouth.

fish.name: Nurse shark
fish.appearance: A blunt snout with barbels on each side; very small eyes; broad, rounded dorsal and anal fins; adults are brown to yellow-brown on top and paler underneath, and juveniles often have black spots; the first dorsal fin starts well behind the pectoral fins; the tail has no distinct lower lobe.
fish.size: Grows to about 9 feet; matures near 6 feet and may live 24 years or more.
fish.range: Nearshore waters along both the Gulf and Atlantic coasts of Florida.
fish.habitat: A common tropical and subtropical coastal shark. Prefers coral reefs, rocky areas and mangrove islands, and often rests motionless on the bottom. Juveniles use shallow reefs, rocky areas, grass flats and mangrove islands as nursery habitat.
habits: A slow, bottom-dwelling shark.
Eats mainly bottom invertebrates such as lobsters, shrimp, crabs, urchins, squid, octopi and mollusks, and occasionally fish, especially grunts.
Mating occurs in summer aggregations.
fish.lookalikes: The lemon shark is similar, but it lacks the nurse shark's barbels.

baits: Cut fish or crab on the bottom
tips: Shark fishing has special gear and handling rules in many places. Check the rules block above and your state agency before you fish for one.
Use a long dehooker and keep your hands away from the mouth.

fish.name: Bonnethead shark
fish.appearance: The head is broadly widened into a shovel shape with no notch at the front midline; the back is gray or grayish-brown, the sides may have small dark spots, and there is no interdorsal ridge.
fish.size: The smallest hammerhead; maximum length about 4 feet; matures around 2 years old at about 3 feet; lifespan estimated at 12 years or more.
fish.range: Native and abundant in nearshore Florida waters.
fish.habitat: Commonly found over shallow sand and mud flats; in colder months it moves into deeper coastal waters.
habits: Feeds mainly on crabs, shrimp, mollusks and small fishes.
Mating occurs in fall, followed by a 4 to 5 month gestation.
baits: Live shrimp or cut bait on light tackle
tips: Considered a good sport fish.
Generally harmless to people, but it can bite if mishandled during catch and release.
fish.lookalikes: Other hammerhead sharks, which grow larger and have hammer-shaped heads.

tips: Use a long dehooker and keep your hands away from the mouth.

fish.name: Bull shark
fish.appearance: Pale to dark gray back fading to a white belly; a bluntly rounded snout much shorter than the mouth is wide; the first dorsal fin has a wide base and begins over or just behind the pectoral fin; the second dorsal fin is much shorter than the first; no interdorsal ridge; a deep, stocky body.
fish.size: Maximum about 10 to 11 feet; matures around 14 to 18 years (about 7 feet) and is estimated to live more than 30 years.
fish.range: Gulf and Atlantic coasts of Florida.
fish.habitat: Estuarine, nearshore and offshore waters. Tolerates a wide range of salinities and often enters freshwater systems; it is the only shark that can tolerate long periods in fresh water, sometimes traveling hundreds of miles inland through coastal rivers.
habits: A versatile, opportunistic feeder: bony fishes, invertebrates, sharks, rays, dolphins, sea turtles and sea birds.
Females give birth to live young in river mouths, shallow estuaries and coastal lagoons.
More aggressive than most sharks and responsible for many unprovoked attacks on humans worldwide.
fish.lookalikes: The lemon shark has first and second dorsal fins that are nearly equal in size; the Caribbean reef shark has an interdorsal ridge; the sandbar shark's first dorsal fin starts before the pectoral fin.

tips: Shark fishing has special gear and handling rules in many places. Check the rules block above and your state agency before you fish for one.
Use a long dehooker and keep your hands away from the mouth.

fish.name: Lemon shark
fish.appearance: A bluntly rounded snout shorter than the width of the mouth; back yellowish-green, brown or olive-gray fading to a white belly; first and second dorsal fins nearly equal in size; no interdorsal ridge.
fish.size: Maximum length about 9 to 10 feet; matures at roughly 11 to 12 years (about 8 feet) and is estimated to live 27 years or more.
fish.habitat: An abundant, inshore tropical shark found in estuarine and nearshore waters of Florida's Gulf and Atlantic coasts. Often enters estuaries and fresh water, but does not travel as far up rivers as the bull shark. Moves south into deeper water in winter. Juveniles use seagrass flats, mangrove forests and tidal creeks as nursery areas.
habits: Feeds on bony fishes, crustaceans, mollusks, rays, small sharks and occasionally seabirds.
Females bear live pups in shallow flats.
Has been involved in only a few non-fatal bites on humans.
fish.lookalikes: The bull shark has unequal first and second dorsal fins; the nurse shark has nasal barbels.

tips: Shark fishing has special gear and handling rules in many places. Check the rules block above and your state agency before you fish for one.
Use a long dehooker and keep your hands away from the mouth.

fish.name: Sand seatrout
fish.appearance: A pale body with a tan or yellowish back fading to a silver or white belly; a pair of large canine teeth at the tip of the upper jaw; yellow inside the mouth; 10 to 12 soft anal fin rays; no dark spots on the back and no barbels on the lower jaw.
fish.size: Usually under 15 inches and about 1 pound.
fish.range: Gulf of Mexico; rare in Atlantic waters.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters over sand bottoms.
habits: Matures in its first or second year.
Spawns inshore over a long season that runs through spring and summer.
Feeds mainly on small fish and shrimp.
fish.lookalikes: The silver seatrout is more silvery and smaller; the silver perch has chin pores and no canine teeth; the weakfish has wavy lines of small, irregular spots on the upper sides.

rigs: A bottom rig or a jig head

fish.name: Black grouper
fish.appearance: Olive or gray with rectangular black blotches and brassy spots; the lower edge of the cheek is gently rounded; the outer third of the second dorsal, anal and tail fins is black; the pectoral fins have a pale yellow or white margin.
fish.size: Up to 48 inches and 180 pounds; commonly up to 40 pounds.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters near structure. Juveniles are found inshore; adults are associated with rocky bottoms, reefs and drop-off walls in water deeper than 60 feet.
habits: Spawns during winter.
Young fish are mostly female and change to male as they grow.
Larger individuals are generally found in deeper water and feed on fish and squid.
baits: Live fish, or dead cut or whole bait
rigs: Heavy tackle is used to bring grouper to the surface
tips: From a boat, baits are typically fished near the bottom.
Grouper are very good to eat.
fish.lookalikes: The gag has a serrated spur on the cheek bone (preopercle); the yellowfin grouper has pectoral fins trimmed in bright yellow.

general.range: Reefs and rocky bottom in the Atlantic and Gulf, mostly in warm water.
general.when: Often best around rocky bottom and ledges offshore.

fish.name: Red grouper
fish.appearance: A brownish-red body with tiny black dots on the snout and a scarlet-orange mouth lining; irregular white blotches on the sides; a long second dorsal fin spine; pectoral fins longer than the pelvic fins; no large black spot on the base of the tail.
fish.size: Up to 42 inches and 50 pounds; commonly around 20 inches and 15 pounds.
fish.habitat: A bottom-dweller over hard and muddy bottoms. Adults and juveniles older than about 6 years are found offshore, while fish aged 1 to 6 years live on nearshore reefs.
habits: Spawns in April and May and prefers water between 66 and 77°F.
Young females change into males as they age.
Lifespan is at least 25 years.
Diet includes a variety of fishes and invertebrates.
fish.lookalikes: The Nassau grouper has a large black spot on the base of the tail.

general.range: Offshore hard bottom in the Gulf and the southern Atlantic.
baits: Cut bait or live fish near the bottom
rigs: A heavy bottom rig
tips: Use strong tackle; groupers dive back to the bottom.

fish.name: Scamp
fish.appearance: A light gray or brown body with dark or reddish-brown spots, often grouped into rosettes; adults have elongated upper and lower tail fin rays; the corners of the mouth may be yellow.
fish.size: Common to 12 inches but may reach up to 42 inches.
fish.habitat: Nearshore and offshore reefs, ledges and rocky bottoms.
habits: Spawns in late spring.
Individuals change sex from female to male as they age.
Feeds on small fishes and invertebrates.
fish.lookalikes: The yellowmouth grouper has yellow inside and at the corners of the mouth.

baits: Live or cut baitfish near the bottom
tips: Use strong tackle; groupers dive back into the rocks.

fish.name: Lionfish
fish.range: Native to the Indo-Pacific and Red Sea; found year-round in Florida waters and from North Carolina to South America, including the Gulf.
fish.habitat: Almost all estuarine and marine habitats, and found in waters up to 1,000 feet deep.
habits: An invasive species that can harm native wildlife and habitat.
Rarely caught on hook and line.
Sometimes caught as bycatch in commercial lobster and stone crab traps.
tips: Spearing and hand-held nets are the most effective ways to harvest them.
Take care when spearfishing so spears don't damage reefs.
They have up to 18 venomous spines on the dorsal, pelvic and anal fins. Stings can cause swelling, blistering, dizziness, tissue death and temporary paralysis.
If stung, soak the wound in hot (not scalding) water for 30 to 90 minutes, and seek medical care if needed.
When filleting, wear puncture-resistant gloves and hold the fish on its side by the gill plates or pectoral fins. Venom stays in the spine bases even after the fish dies.
Do not touch one with bare hands, even a dead fish.

general.appearance: Small to medium-size reef fish, often with yellow or blue stripes, that make a grunting sound.
general.range: Reefs, docks, bridges and mangroves, mostly in warm water.
habits: They often gather in schools near structure.
rigs: A light bottom rig with a small hook
tips: A good fish for beginners.
Often caught to use as bait for bigger fish.

general.appearance: A silvery jack with a dark stripe running along the back and onto the lower lobe of the tail.
general.range: Reefs and open water in warm Atlantic and Gulf waters.
habits: They travel in schools.
tips: They fight hard for their size.

general.appearance: A bottom-dwelling fish with a broad, flat head, a wide mouth and mottled coloring.
general.range: Shallow bays, grass flats and areas around structure, mostly in the Gulf.
habits: They live on or near the bottom and hide in holes and debris.
baits: Shrimp or cut bait on the bottom
tips: Often caught by accident while fishing the bottom for other species.
Handle with care; they bite.

fish.name: White catfish
fish.appearance: Sides blue-gray to blue-black, sometimes mottled; the tail is moderately forked.
fish.habitat: Found statewide in rivers, streams and slightly brackish coastal waters.
habits: Fish make up most of the diet, but whites also eat larval aquatic insects, small crustaceans, fish eggs and aquatic plants.
They may feed at night but are less nocturnal than other catfish.
baits: Live minnows and worms account for most catches; whites also take cut and prepared baits
tips: Among Florida catfish, whites are second only to channel catfish in popularity.
fish.lookalikes: The anal fin is shorter and rounder than on channel or blue catfish.

general.when: Often best at dusk and at night.
rigs: A bottom rig with a sliding sinker
tips: Handle with care: the spines are sharp.

fish.name: Brown bullhead
fish.appearance: Chin barbels are pigmented (not whitish as on yellow bullheads); irregular brownish mottling over a light background on the sides, a creamy white belly and a square tail.
fish.habitat: Still or slowly flowing warm water, including ponds, lakes, reservoirs, large rivers and sluggish streams.
habits: Mainly bottom feeders that feed mostly at night.
Sensitive barbels help them find food such as insects, plant material, carrion, small fish, snails, crayfish, worms and leeches.
fish.when: They bite throughout the day, but fishing is best at night.
baits: Worms, minnows, shrimp, chicken innards and stinkbaits
tips: Fair fighters and easy to catch.
fish.lookalikes: Yellow bullheads have whitish chin barbels rather than pigmented ones.

general.range: Ponds, lakes and slow rivers across much of the eastern United States.
rigs: A bottom rig with a small sinker
tips: Handle with care: the spines are sharp.

fish.name: Yellow bullhead
fish.appearance: Similar to the brown bullhead, but with light-colored chin barbels and usually lighter overall.
fish.habitat: Varies; includes vegetated areas of clear, shallow lakes, reservoirs, ponds and slow-flowing streams. It tolerates polluted water better than most catfish.
habits: A scavenger that prefers minnows, snails, shrimp and crayfish.
baits: Cut bait, live worms, crickets, doughballs and a wide variety of natural and prepared baits
tips: Easy to catch.
fish.lookalikes: The brown bullhead; the yellow bullhead usually has light chin barbels and lighter coloration.

general.range: Ponds, lakes and slow streams across much of the eastern United States.
rigs: A bottom rig with a small sinker
tips: Handle with care: the spines are sharp.

fish.name: Blue catfish
fish.appearance: Adults are stout with a noticeably humped back in front of the dorsal fin; the back and upper sides are blue to slate gray and the belly is white.
fish.range: Listed by FWC as a nonnative species in Florida. Originally found in the Escambia and Yellow rivers in northwest Florida; now also in the Apalachicola and Suwannee rivers.
fish.habitat: Big rivers and the lower reaches of major tributaries; they prefer clearer, faster-moving water, usually over sand, gravel or rock bottoms.
habits: Young blues eat aquatic insects and small fish; larger blues prefer crayfish, mussels and other fish.
baits: Cut fish and stinkbaits rigged on large hooks
rigs: Heavy lead sinkers with large hooks. Blues are also caught on bush hooks or trotlines, as well as with rod and reel.
tips: Considered one of the strongest freshwater fish.
Most are caught by bottom fishing.
fish.lookalikes: Blues resemble channel catfish, with deeply forked tails. Unlike channel catfish, blues lack spots and have a longer, straight-edged anal fin.

general.when: Often best at dusk and at night.
tips: Handle with care: the spines are sharp.

fish.name: Flathead catfish
fish.appearance: A flattened head, small eyes, a squarish tail and a lower jaw that juts out; yellow-brown, often mottled on top, with a cream-colored belly.
fish.range: Listed by FWC as a nonnative species in Florida. Found in the Apalachicola and Escambia rivers, where it recently arrived from Georgia and Alabama.
fish.habitat: Long, slow-moving rivers that are moderately murky.
habits: Lives alone.
Spawns in late spring; a parent digs a nest in a natural cavity or beside a large submerged object, and the male guards and fans the golden-yellow eggs.
Feeds mainly on other fish, especially catfish and sunfish.
fish.when: Bites best at night in shallow water while hunting for food.
rigs: Heavy tackle, fished on the bottom
tips: Its solitary habit makes it harder to catch than other catfish.
Handle with care: the spines are sharp.

fish.name: Florida gar
fish.appearance: Bony, armor-like scales that interlock; irregular round spots cover the head, body and fins.
fish.range: The Ochlockonee River and waters east and south in peninsular Florida.
fish.habitat: Streams, canals and lakes with mud or sand bottoms, usually near underwater vegetation.
habits: Gulps air using an air bladder when oxygen is low.
In late winter and early spring, both sexes gather in shallow, weedy water to spawn.
Adults mainly eat fish, shrimp and crayfish.
baits: Minnows, artificial lures, or frayed nylon cord that tangles in the gar's teeth
rigs: Gar can also be taken with bow and arrow, gigs or snag hooks
tips: Described as strong, sporty fighters.
Check the rules block above before using a bow, gig or snag hook.

fish.name: Oscar
fish.appearance: Young fish have wavy white and orange markings on a black background. Adults are olive blue-green and mustard with large dark blotches and a bright red eyespot near the base of the upper tail fin; a stouter, more oval body than native bream and a thick mucus coat.
fish.size: Two-pound fish are considered large. Oscars caught in the Everglades average about 10 inches and three-quarters of a pound.
fish.range: Most abundant in canals of water conservation areas and Everglades habitats in Collier, western Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach counties; found throughout south Florida but usually less abundant outside marsh-related canals. The native range is the Orinoco, La Plata and Amazon river basins in South America.
fish.habitat: Most successful in canals running through marshes; found in smaller numbers in coastal canals, ponds and lakes from central Florida southward.
habits: Spawn on flat, solid surfaces when the water warms to about 82 to 91°F; a female lays roughly 3,000 eggs, and both parents may guard young in shallow shoreline water.
Feed mainly on small fish, insects and crustaceans.
baits: Cut fish, cut shrimp, crickets and worms
The best artificial options are small jigs tipped with cut bait and small spinnerbaits
tips: Fly fishing can also be productive.
A hard-fighting, panfish-type fishery that is boom-and-bust because of periodic winterkills; when fish are abundant, catch rates are exceptional.

fish.name: Walking catfish

source.label: USGS NAS fact sheet: Walking Catfish

fish.appearance: A long, eel-like body. Florida's original imports were albino, but wild fish have mostly reverted to dark brown to gray.
fish.size: Grows to about 61 cm in its native range and is rarely that large.
fish.range: Native to southeastern Asia. In the United States it is established only in Florida, mostly in the southern half of the state; records in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Massachusetts, Nevada and Guam are listed as failed introductions.
fish.habitat: Low-oxygen waters, canal networks in southeastern Florida, temporary wetlands and seasonal pools, and aquaculture ponds. Cold snaps can cause die-offs.
habits: Can breathe air, which helps it survive in low-oxygen water.
Moves overland, especially on rainy nights, which speeds its spread between water bodies.
Adults guard free-swimming young.
Preys on fish and tadpoles.
Imported to Florida in the early 1960s for the aquarium trade.

baits: Worms, cut bait or shrimp on the bottom
tips: Handle with care: the spines are sharp.
Non-native fish can have special rules; check the rules block above.

fish.name: Clown knifefish

source.label: USGS NAS fact sheet: Clown Knifefish

fish.appearance: A long anal fin that joins the tail fin separates it from North American native freshwater fishes. Selective breeding has produced several color varieties.
fish.size: Can reach about 100 cm and roughly 5 kg; slightly smaller in Florida.
fish.range: Native to tropical Asia. Established in Florida (seven drainages, including the Everglades, Lake Okeechobee and Tampa Bay); other records exist in Hawaii, New York, Texas and a few other states.
fish.habitat: Lakes and deeper river pools, usually near submerged structure such as rocks, wood and aquatic plants, which serve as daytime cover and spawning substrate.
habits: Carnivorous: eats crustaceans, insects and fishes.
Nocturnal.
Spawns from March to July; eggs are laid on submerged wood and one parent guards the eggs and fry.
Probably released from the aquarium trade.
tips: Anglers in Florida's Palm Beach County target the local population for sport, sometimes with guides who specialize in non-native fish.
fish.lookalikes: Often misidentified as Chitala chitala.

fish.name: Sailfin catfish (suckermouth)

source.label: USGS NAS fact sheet: Vermiculated Sailfin Catfish

fish.appearance: A suckermouth armored catfish with flexible bony plates and a ventral sucking mouth. The back has light spots that become chevron shapes toward the tail, and the belly has dark and light bands of equal width.
fish.size: Can reach about 70 cm.
fish.range: Native to the Madeira River drainage in the Amazon basin. Established in Florida and recently spreading into new drainages; also recorded in several other states.
fish.habitat: Natural streams and artesian springs in Florida; tolerates mildly brackish water for extended periods.
habits: A bottom forager that attaches to surfaces with its mouth and eats detritus and algae.
In wintering artesian springs it grazes organisms growing on Florida manatees.
Males dig burrows in riverbanks where females lay and guard eggs.
fish.lookalikes: Often confused with Hypostomus. Native North American catfishes lack the bony plates and suckermouth of these armored catfishes.

tips: Rarely a target for anglers.
Handle with care: the spines are sharp.

fish.name: Brown hoplo

source.label: USGS NAS fact sheet: Brown Hoplo

fish.size: Reaches about 22 cm standard length; males are larger than females.
fish.range: Native to tropical America. Established in Florida across much of the peninsula, as far north as Duval County near Jacksonville; also records in Georgia.
fish.habitat: Slow-moving rivers, canals, streams and pools. It breathes air, so it survives in low-oxygen water such as seasonal Florida wetlands, and tolerates fresh and brackish water.
habits: A benthic scavenger that eats small crustaceans, aquatic insect larvae, detritus and plant matter.
In Florida, spawning runs from May to September; males build bubble nests.
Males use enlarged pectoral spines in aggressive or defensive encounters.
tips: A small commercial and recreational castnet fishery has developed in Florida.

baits: Worms or small pieces of cut bait

fish.name: Peacock bass

source.label: USGS NAS fact sheet: Butterfly Peacock Bass

fish.size: Maximum about 70 cm total length.
fish.range: Native to tropical South America. Established in south Florida, with fishable populations in more than 500 km of canals and urban lakes around Miami and Fort Lauderdale; cold winters limit its range to the southernmost counties. Also established in Hawaii, Puerto Rico and Guam.
fish.habitat: Canals, urban lakes and reservoirs.
habits: A large daytime (diurnal) predator that eats a wide variety of prey, including native fishes in Florida.
A pair-forming substrate spawner: adults spawn on flat surfaces and move the hatched larvae to nests in shallow depressions, or on rocks or logs.
Cold winters are not survivable, which limits its range.
tips: Valued as a sport fish; Florida has an established fishery in its southeast canals.
fish.lookalikes: Other Cichla species and hybrids between them are often mistaken for the butterfly peacock bass.

tips: Look for them near cover along canal edges.

fish.name: Tilapia (blue)

source.label: USGS NAS fact sheet: Blue Tilapia

fish.appearance: Breeding males show metallic blue coloration. Adults have 15 to 16 dorsal spines and 27 to 30 total dorsal fin rays, a vermilion dorsal fin margin and no distinct stripes on the tail fin.
fish.size: Up to about 51 cm long.
fish.range: Native to Africa and the Middle East. Established in Arizona, California, Florida, Nevada, North Carolina and Texas; in Florida it has been considered the most widespread foreign fish for over a decade.
fish.habitat: Thrives in brackish water; has colonized heated power-plant effluent ponds, streams, reservoirs and a spring run in Nevada. It does not survive cold winters in most of the United States.
habits: Competes with native fish for spawning areas, food and space.
Eats aquatic vegetation and is linked to predation on native fish.
fish.lookalikes: The Nile tilapia has more dorsal spines (16 to 18), distinct dark stripes on the tail fin, red male breeding color and a dark dorsal fin margin.

baits: Worms, bread or corn on a small hook
tips: Non-native fish can have special rules; check the rules block above.

fish.name: Mayan cichlid

source.label: USGS NAS fact sheet: Mayan Cichlid

fish.appearance: Yellow to olive-brown with five to seven dark vertical bars and a dark spot ringed in blue at the base of the tail; a slightly protrusible mouth with several rows of teeth, including canine-like teeth at the front.
fish.size: Can reach about 22 cm.
fish.range: Native to Atlantic-slope drainages from Mexico south to Nicaragua. Established in southern Florida (22 watersheds, including the Everglades, Lake Okeechobee, Kissimmee and Tampa Bay) and still spreading.
fish.habitat: Rivers, lakes, ponds, marshes and estuaries; tolerates fresh, brackish and marine water. In Florida it occupies mangrove fringes and inland areas near estuaries.
habits: A generalist predator: adults eat mostly fish in the dry season, plus algae, snails, crustaceans and insects.
Both parents guard the nest and the young. In southern Florida nests are shallow depressions in red mangrove roots, with spawning peaking from about April to June.
Tolerates wide temperature and salinity ranges and can survive very low oxygen for a couple of hours.
tips: Among the most abundant fish in angler catches in some Everglades canals.
fish.lookalikes: Often confused with sunfishes and black basses. Cichlids have a single nostril on each side of the head and a broken lateral line; sunfishes and black basses have two nostrils and a continuous lateral line.

baits: Worms, small shrimp or cut bait
rigs: A small hook with a split shot

fish.name: Black bullhead

source.label: USGS NAS fact sheet: Black Bullhead

fish.appearance: Dark chin barbels, a slightly notched tail fin, a short rounded anal fin with 19 to 23 rays, and a uniform body color with no mottling.
fish.size: Grows up to about 62 cm (24 inches) total length.
fish.range: Native to the Great Lakes, Hudson Bay and Mississippi River basins and Gulf Slope drainages from Mobile Bay to northern Mexico. Introduced and established in many other states, mostly in the West.
habits: Described as a voracious predator of newly hatched gamefish.
In Arizona it forms large, stunted populations that compete with more desirable fishes.
tips: Was intentionally stocked in some places as a sport fish and a food fish.
fish.lookalikes: The yellow bullhead has white or yellow barbels, a straight tail-fin margin and 24 to 27 anal fin rays. The brown bullhead has brown or black mottling and a barbel that reaches the pectoral fin.

general.habitat: Muddy ponds, lakes and slow streams.
general.when: Often best at night.
baits: Worms, minnows or stinkbait on the bottom
tips: Handle with care: the spines are sharp.

fish.name: Spotted gar

source.label: USGS NAS fact sheet: Spotted Gar

fish.size: The page gives a maximum size of 112 cm.
fish.range: Native from the Lake Erie and southern Lake Michigan drainages south through the Mississippi River basin to the Gulf Coast, including Gulf Slope drainages from the lower Apalachicola River in Florida to the Nueces River in Texas. Reported as introduced in several other states.

general.appearance: A long, narrow fish with a toothy snout, armor-like scales and dark spots over the head, body and fins.
general.habitat: Quiet, weedy water in lakes, sloughs and slow rivers.
habits: It gulps air at the surface.
baits: Frayed nylon rope, which tangles in the teeth
tips: Check the rules block above; gar rules vary by state.

general.appearance: A long, slender fish with a snake-like head and a large dark spot with a light ring near the tail.
general.range: Canals and ponds in southeast Florida, where it is non-native.
habits: It breathes air and can survive in low-oxygen water.
It is a predator.
tips: It is an invasive fish. Check the rules block above and your state's rules on handling and releasing it.

general.appearance: A small bullhead catfish with a flattened head and sharp spines.
general.range: Slow streams and ponds in the Southeast.
baits: Worms or stinkbait on the bottom
tips: Handle with care: the spines are sharp.

general.appearance: A small bullhead catfish with sharp spines.
general.range: Streams and ponds in the Southeast.
general.habitat: Slow water with a soft bottom.
baits: Worms or stinkbait on the bottom
tips: Handle with care: the spines are sharp.

general.appearance: A small bullhead catfish with pale spots on its sides and sharp spines.
general.range: Rivers and streams in north Florida and the Southeast.
baits: Worms or stinkbait on the bottom
tips: Handle with care: the spines are sharp.

general.appearance: A small catfish with a forked tail and sharp spines.
general.range: Streams in Texas, New Mexico and northern Mexico.
general.habitat: Clear streams with gravel or rock bottoms.
baits: Worms, minnows or stinkbait on the bottom
tips: Handle with care: the spines are sharp.

general.appearance: A very long, narrow snout with many sharp teeth, and spotted fins.
general.range: Rivers, lakes and brackish water across the eastern and central United States.
habits: It gulps air at the surface.
baits: Frayed nylon rope, which tangles in the teeth
tips: Check the rules block above; gar rules vary by state.

fish.name: Knobbed porgy
fish.appearance: Deep-bodied and silver with a reddish tint; a very steep forehead, and adults have a strongly projecting nape; the head is dark purplish-gray with yellowish-bronze spots; a large blue spot at the base of the pectoral fin.
fish.size: Up to 21 inches.
fish.range: North Carolina to south Florida, and throughout the Gulf of Mexico.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters over hard bottoms.
habits: Feeds mainly on invertebrates.
fish.lookalikes: The littlehead porgy has many wavy, dark blue lines on its snout.

rigs: A bottom rig with a small hook

fish.name: Red porgy
fish.appearance: Pinkish-silver head and body with several tiny blue spots; yellow around the eyes and snout; a rounded head. It is the only Florida porgy with a round rear nostril.
fish.size: Up to 36 inches.
fish.habitat: Coastal waters over rocky or sandy bottoms.
habits: Feeds on fish and invertebrates.
fish.lookalikes: Other porgies have slit-like rear nostrils.

rigs: A bottom rig with a small hook

fish.name: Rock hind
fish.appearance: Usually pale with red-to-brown spots on the body, fins and tail; the color can vary.
fish.range: One of the most common groupers along the Texas Gulf Coast.
fish.habitat: Near jetties and on snapper banks.

baits: Cut bait or small live fish near the bottom
tips: Use strong tackle; groupers dive back into the rocks.

general.appearance: A small, silvery, deep-bodied fish with a mouth that points downward and can stretch out to feed on the bottom.
general.range: Shallow bays, grass flats, mangrove shorelines and inshore waters along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, mostly in warm water.
general.habitat: Sandy and grassy flats and muddy, mangrove-lined areas.
habits: They travel in schools.
They feed on the bottom.
baits: A very small hook with a tiny piece of shrimp
Cast nets and sabiki rigs are often used instead of a hook
tips: Often caught to use as live bait for larger fish such as snook, trout and redfish.
general.lookalikes: Several mojarra species look alike, including the silver jenny and the spotfin mojarra.
